data.source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
data.locator: Methods, PReS screening timing; Results, screening time and cohort flow.
data.source_setting: Adult acute medical/surgical wards at a large Australian tertiary hospital; weekday screen for rehabilitation needs, linked to physician assessment and potential acute in-reach or subacute inpatient rehabilitation.
data.source_n: 4,000 consecutive screening episodes; acute ward subgroup n=2,949; the article reports n=1,604 screened in the day 5-7 target window.
data.quantity: Screening achieved in target window (days 5-7 after acute admission) among acute ward admissions
data.source_evidence_basis: The article states that screening for acute-ward patients was achieved within days 5-7 in 86.9% of cases and gives n=1,604. The methods specify day 5, shifting to the next weekday when it falls on a weekend.
data.limitations: The reported numerator and percentage do not arithmetically match the stated subgroup denominator (1,604/2,949 is not 86.9%); retain the published values as reported and resolve denominator from the source figure before quantitative calibration. Single Australian site, under-75 cohort; this was a screening service rather than universal multidisciplinary assessment.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Model screening due dates, weekend deferral, missed-record retry, and referral/physician assessment as separate steps. Treat the reported rate as a workflow signal pending denominator resolution, not a transferable local probability.

data.source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
data.locator: Results, screening timing among patients screened after ICU transfer.
data.source_setting: Same Australian acute hospital PReS service; ICU survivors screened after return to acute ward.
data.source_n: 1,051 screening episodes after transfer from ICU.
data.quantity: Median time from hospital admission to screening for patients screened after ICU transfer
data.source_evidence_basis: The primary article reports a median of nine days from admission to screening for the ICU-transfer subgroup, with an interquartile range of seven to fifteen days.
data.limitations: Conditional ICU subgroup at one hospital; this is time to a screening episode, not time to full rehabilitation assessment or treatment. Not a US or RWJ estimate.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Allow ICU transfer and return-to-ward to reset screening eligibility, and distinguish screening delay from clinical assessment, acceptance, and first treatment.

data.source_title: Targeted rehabilitation may improve patient flow and outcomes: development and implementation of a novel Proactive Rehabilitation Screening (PReS) service
data.locator: Results and Table 1, screening duration across ten consecutive weekdays.
data.source_setting: Same Australian acute hospital; rehabilitation nurse performed weekday PReS case finding using medical records.
data.source_period: Ten consecutive weekdays within the May 2017-February 2019 service period; exact dates not stated in the cited text.
data.source_n: 158 screening episodes observed across 10 weekdays; 561 total minutes.
data.quantity: Mean staff time per screening episode
data.source_evidence_basis: The observed total was 561 minutes for 158 screenings over ten weekdays, reported by the authors as an average of 3.6 minutes per screening.
data.limitations: This is chart-screening workload, not multidisciplinary bedside assessment or therapy time. Single service, paper records, and only ten observed days; no distribution is reported.
data.inferred_scenario_use: Keep case-finding labor separate from rehabilitation physician/therapist assessment and treatment resources. Use only as an external screening-workload reference.
